html:
Preliminaries

This chapter will present an overview of background material in complex dynamics that shall be of importance to us later. The content here has found excellent footings in (Milnor 2011), (McMullen 2016), and (Carleson and Gamelin 2013). Throughout this chapter, \(f: S \rightarrow S\) is a holomorphic function and \(S\) a Riemann surface (unless otherwise stated).

By a Riemann surface \(S\), we mean a connected complex analytic manifold of complex dimension \(1\). In particular, S is a topological manifold of dimension 2 with the transition maps being holomorphic (after appropriately identifying domains in \(\mathbb{R}^2\) with domains in \(\mathbb{C}\)). A function \(f: S \rightarrow S'\) between Riemann surfaces \(S\) and \(S'\) is said to be holomorphic if it is so with respect to the local coordinate maps. If \(S = S'\) we shall call \(f\) a self map. These self maps induce the concept of change via iteration. For instance, the map \((z \rightarrow z^2) : (1 - \frac{1}{n})\mathbb{D} \rightarrow (1 - \frac{1}{n})\mathbb{D}\) (upon iteration) eventually gobbles up the entire disk of radius \(1 - \frac{1}{n}\), whereas the map \((z \rightarrow z^2) : \mathbb{D} \rightarrow \mathbb{D}\) keeps the unit disk as it is. These examples illustrate drastically different dynamics on two Riemann surfaces by the same map, despite one being \(\frac{1}{n}\)-close to the other for arbitrarily large \(n\).

Now, given that there are uncountably many Riemann surfaces and that studying dynamics on one gives no approximate information about the dynamics on the other, the problem of classifying Riemann surfaces must be dealt with first. Covering space theory shall aid us in this, reason being, Riemann surfaces (by definition) are semi-locally simply connected and locally path-connected and hence admit universal covers. Let \(S\) be a Riemann surface with the universal cover \(p : \hat{S} \rightarrow S\), then \(p\) is a normal cover, hence, \(S \cong \hat{S}/G\), where \(G\) is a subgroup of Aut\((\hat{S})\) that acts freely and properly discontinuously on \(\hat{S}\). With the help of the following theorem (Forster 2012) one can lift the identification above to the category of Riemann surfaces.

Theorem 2.1

(Category Lifting):- Let \(S\) be a Riemann surface with \(p: \hat{S} \rightarrow S\) a topological covering map. Then there exists a unique complex structure on \(\hat{S}\) that turns the map \(p\) into a holomorphic covering map.

Note that, given a Riemann surface \(S\), the moment one has \(S \cong \hat{S}/G\), one can forget about \(S\) because the identification of the complex structures of \(S\) and \(\hat{S}\) via quotients is done in a well-defined manner. Therefore, to classify Riemann surfaces one must classify simply-connected Riemann surfaces and the discrete subgroups of its respective automorphism groups1. By a theorem of Poincaré and Koebe (Varolin 2011) we know that there are only three simply connected Riemann surfaces (upto conformal equivalence), stated explicitly:-

Theorem 2.2

(Uniformization Theorem):- Any simply connected Riemann surface is conformally isomorphic to one of the following:-

  1. The complex plane \(\mathbb{C}\), consisting of complex numbers \(z = x+iy\).

  2. The unit disk \(\mathbb{D}\), consisting of complex numbers with norm \(<1\).

  3. The Riemann sphere \(\hat{\mathbb{C}}\), consisting of \(\mathbb{C}\) together with \(\infty\), wherein \(w = 1/z\) is a coordinate map in a neighbourhood around \(\infty\).

Riemann surfaces that admit \(\mathbb{C},\hat{\mathbb{C}}\), and \(\mathbb{D}\) as its universal cover are called Euclidean, Spherical, and Hyperbolic (respectively). If \(G <\) Aut\((\hat{\mathbb{C})}\) acts properly discontinuously then by compactness \(G = {0}\). Therefore, there is only one Spherical surface, and that is the Riemann sphere. Similarly, one can handle the case of Euclidean surfaces by noting that \(G <\) Aut\((\mathbb{C}) (\cong \mathbb{C}^*\times\mathbb{C})\) is abelian and torsion free, and as the action of \(G\) on \(\mathbb{C}\) is a covering space action, it can’t have rank \(\geq 3\), for the orbits of points in \(\mathbb{C}\) will then be dense. So, \(G\) is isomorphic to \({0}\), \(\mathbb{Z}\), or \(\mathbb{Z}\times\mathbb{Z}\). Finally, upto equivalence, we have the following surfaces to study - the Riemann sphere, the complex plane, torus, cylinder (or the punctured plane), and hyperbolic surfaces. Of these, hyperbolic surfaces offer significantly more mathematical information to dynamics than the others in the lot.

So, let us handle hyperbolic surfaces first. We propose to do that by answering the following questions:-

  1. Why care about hyperbolic surfaces?

  2. What are some of its relevant features?

  3. What has all this got to do with complex dynamics?

The answer to the first question is rather simple - hyperbolic surfaces are found in abundance. As can be inferred from the discussion above, all Riemann surfaces with non-abelian fundamental group must be hyperbolic. In fact, there are only 4 Riemann surfaces (upto equivalence) that aren’t hyperbolic. In addition, it must also noted that a sufficiently small domain of a given Riemann surface is hyperbolic. Indeed, fix a Riemann surface \(S\), if \(S\) is not hyperbolic then \(S\) is one of the four model surfaces, deleting three points from any of them would leave a non-abelian fundamental group, hence the resulting surface must certainly be hyperbolic. If \(S\) was hyperbolic to begin with and you delete two points from it, it can’t be compact, hence it must either be the plane or the punctured plane. It can’t be the plane, for \(S\) must then be simply-connected, and the fundamental group of a doubly punctured disk isn’t abelian. It can’t be a punctured plane, for lifting the inclusion map \(S\backslash\{p, q\} \hookrightarrow S\) to its respective universal covers would yield a non-trivial holomorphic map from \(\mathbb{C}\) to \(\mathbb{D}\) contradicting Liouville’s Theorem. Therefore, any Riemann surface with three or more punctures is hyperbolic.

It is a brilliant insight of Riemann that to be able to do geometry on a manifold \(M\) one basically needs a symmetric, positive definite, bilinear form on the tangent space \(T_pM\) that varies smoothly with \(p\). Such inner-products lead to distances, geodesics, angles, curvature, and they can be easily arranged (by locally pushing metrics on \(\mathbb{R}^n\) to \(M\), and patching it up via partitions of unity). To answer the second question one needs to introduce some such geometry in the setup. Hence, we will be interested in imposing a Riemannian manifold structure on our hyperbolic surface \(S\), but not through arbitrary metrics; we will demand this change of category to preserve Aut\((S)\) as Riemann surfaces. Let us first impose such a metric on \(\mathbb{H}\), the Poincaré upper-half plane, and later filter it for its quotients.

Theorem 2.3

(Poincaré Metric on \(\mathbb{H}\)):- There exists a unique (upto multiplication by a constant) Riemannian metric on \(\mathbb{H}\) which is invariant under all elements of Aut\((\mathbb{H})\).

So, all elements \(g \in\) Aut\((\mathbb{H})\) under such an invariant metric shall be isometries of \(\mathbb{H}\). This is an instance of a general correspondence between Lie groups and symmetric spaces. In that, any left invariant metric on the Lie group turns it into a symmetric space, and the group of isometries of a symmetric space naturally admits a Lie group structure.

A symmetric Riemannian metric looks like - \(g_{11}dx\otimes dx + 2g_{12}dx\otimes dy + g_{22}dy\otimes dy\). Now, given a conformal map, \(f = u + iv\), which transfers the \((dx, dy)\) tangent plane to \((du, dv)\) tangent plane, we have, \[\begin{pmatrix} du\\dv \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} u_x & u_y\\ v_x & v_y \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} dx\\dy \end{pmatrix}\]

Cauchy-Riemann equations yield the following form for the metric altered by \(f\) \[du\otimes du + dv\otimes dv = (u_x^2 + v_x^2)dx\otimes dx + (u_y^2 + v_y^2)dy\otimes dy\]

Thus the following definition is very natural.

Definition 2.4

(Conformal Metric):- A metric \(ds^2\) (which stands for \(ds\otimes ds\)) \(= g_{11}dx^2 + 2g_{12}dxdy + g_{22}dy^2\) will be called conformal iff \(g_{11} = g_{22}\) and \(g_{12} = 0\).

The invariant metric on \(\mathbb{H}\) whose existence is guaranteed by Theorem 2.3 turns out to be conformal, hence it must be unique upto multiplication by a constant. A conformal metric looks like \(ds^2 = \gamma(x+iy)^2(dx^2 + dy^2)\), the norm on tangents given by such a metric will be of the form - \(\gamma(x+iy)\sqrt{dx^2 + dy^2} = \gamma(z)|dz|\). Using the Cayley transform \(\frac{z+i}{z-i}\), one can transfer the invariant metric on \(\mathbb{H}\) to an invariant metric on \(\mathbb{D}\), which will then take the form \(ds = (\frac{2}{1 -|z|^2})|dz|\). Let us use this to construct a metric on \(\mathbb{D}/\Gamma\), where \(\Gamma <\) Aut\((\mathbb{D})\) (\(\cong PSL_2(\mathbb{R})\)) is discrete.

Let \(S\) be a hyperbolic surface and \(p: \mathbb{D} \rightarrow S\) be its universal cover. For \(y \in S\), let \(U_y\) be an evenly covered neighbourhood of \(y\) in \(S\). Choose \(V_a\) open in \(\mathbb{D}\) such that \(p_{\big|V_a}: V_a \rightarrow U_y\) is a biholomorphism. Set \(\gamma_a(p_{\big|V_a}) = \frac{\rho(z)}{|p'(z)|}\), where \(\rho(z)|dz|\) is the invariant metric on \(\mathbb{D}\). Patch it up via \(\{\xi_y\}_y\) (a partition of unity subordinate to the open cover \(\{U_y\}_y\)) by setting the following metric on \(S\):- \[ds^2 = \sum_{y}{\xi_y(\gamma_a(p_{\big|V_a}(z)))^2(dx^2 +dy^2)}\]

It remains to check that the pushforward metric is well-defined. Let \(x,a \in p^{-1}(y)\), since \(p\) is a normal covering, \(\exists \phi\), \(\phi: \mathbb{D} \rightarrow \mathbb{D}\), a deck transformation such that \(p = \phi \circ p\) and \(\phi(x) = a\). Chain rule and the fact that \(\phi\) is a Möbius transformation gives:- \[p'(a) = p'(x)\phi'(a),\] \[|\phi'(a)| = \frac{1 - |x|^2}{1 - |a|^2} = \frac{\rho(a)}{\rho(x)}\]

Therefore, \[\frac{\rho(a)}{|p'(a)|} = \frac{\rho(x)}{|p'(x)|}\]

\(\Rightarrow \gamma_a(p_{\big|V_a}(z)) = \gamma_x(p_{\big|V_x}(z))\). This induced Riemannian metric on the hyperbolic surface \(S\) shall be referred to as the Poincaré metric which shall lead to (as was pointed before) distances, geodesics, angles, and curvature.

Lemma 2.5

(Completeness Lemma):- Let \(S\) be a hyperbolic surface and let dist\(_S\) denote the Poincaré distance on \(S\). Then:-

  1. \((S,\) dist\(_S)\) is a complete metric space.

  2. There exists a geodesic joining any two points of \(S\).

Finally, we can disclose the answer to the second question. Hyperbolic surfaces endowed with this specific negatively curved geometry obey a marvellous non-increasing under holomorphic maps property.

Theorem 2.6

(Pick’s Theorem):- Let \(S\), \(S'\) be hyperbolic and \(f: S \rightarrow S'\) be holomorphic. Then:-

  1. \(f\) is a conformal isomorphism, in particular an isometry.

  2. \(f\) is a covering map, that is, a local isometry.

  3. \(\forall\) compacts \(K\), \(f_{\big|K}\) is a contraction mapping.

Post Pick’s Theorem the reason hyperbolic spaces are relevant to dynamics become evident2. Let us embark on that journey but also parallelly get some mathematical understanding of the words - order, chaos, and dynamics.

In this subject one is interested in studying how iterates of a self map \(f\) deform the surface \(S\). This amounts to studying the orbits of individual points under \(f\), that is, the sequence - \(\{f^{\circ n}(z)\}_n\), for a given \(z \in S\). For instance, consider the map \((z \rightarrow z^n): \mathbb{C} \rightarrow \mathbb{C}\), it is visually clear that on the set of points with norm either \((< 1)\) or \((> 1)\), the iterates of the map behave in a stable and predictable manner. Indeed, if one embeds \(\mathbb{C} \hookrightarrow \hat{\mathbb{C}}\), then it can easily be seen that the points \(0\) and \(\infty\) uniformly attract the points in the set mentioned above. But the points on the unit circle with irrational arguments are spun across in an erratic manner. Therefore, to capture both the following should be expected:-

Definition 2.7

(Normal Family):- A sequence \(\{f_i\}_i\) of holomorphic functions from a Riemann surface \(S\) to a Riemann surface \(T\) will be said to converge locally uniformly if for every point of \(S\) one has a neighbourhood \(N\) such that the sequence \(\{f_i\big|_N\}_i\) converges uniformly (or equivalently, it converges uniformly on compacts). The same sequence will be said to diverge locally uniformly from \(T\) if for every compact set \(K \subset S\) and \(K' \subset T\), \(f_n(K)\) and \(K'\) are eventually disjoint. A collection \(\mathcal{F}\) of holomorphic maps between \(S\) and \(T\) will be called normal if for every infinite sequence of \(\mathcal{F}\) we have a subsequence that either converges locally uniformly or diverges locally uniformly.

With this definition we have the following two crucial lemmas as consequences of Pick’s Theorem.

Lemma 2.8

(Hyperbolic Compactness):- If \(S\) and \(T\) are hyperbolic, then every family \(\mathcal{F}\) of holomorphic maps from \(S\) to \(T\) is normal.

Lemma 2.9

(Ball Convergence):- Suppose \(S \subset S'\) are Riemann surfaces with \(S\) hyperbolic. Given a sequence of points \(\{p_n\}_n\) which converges (in \(S'\)) to a boundary point \(\hat{p} \in \partial S\). For any fixed \(r\), one has that the entire neighbourhood of balls of radius \(r\) around points in \(\{p_n\}_n\) converge uniformly to \(\hat{p}\).

These two lemmas shall be exploited vehemently for they say something phenomenal about the dynamics of hyperbolic surfaces. They say that self maps on hyperbolic surfaces show no chaotic behaviour whatsoever, even along the boundary! This knowledge about stability on hyperbolic domains will be used to study stability of deformations in general. Thus, hyperbolic surfaces are not only objects of study but also tools in themselves.

The stage is now ripe to formally introduce stability, chaos, dynamics, and state the classification theorem for dynamics on hyperbolic surfaces.

Definition 2.10

(Stability):- Given a holomorphic function \(f: S\rightarrow S\) on a Riemann surface \(S\). Let \(F(f)\), the Fatou set of \(f\) be the union of all open sets \(U \subseteq S\) such that \(\{f_{\big|U}^{\circ n}\}_n\) is a normal family. We say that \(f\) deforms the set \(F(f)\) in a stable manner.

Definition 2.11

(Chaos):- Given a holomorphic function \(f: S\rightarrow S\) on a Riemann surface \(S\). Let \(J(f) := S\backslash F(f)\) be the Julia set of \(f\). Then we say that \(f\) deforms the set \(J(f)\) chaotically.

By dynamics, we mean the structure of the sets \(J(f)\) and \(F(f)\), be it in the category of sets, topological spaces, Riemann surfaces, or Riemannian manifolds. Having introduced normality as the right means to capture stability let us probe further on what means one should adopt to study dynamics on a given surface.

There is a general philosophy which speaks of orbits of critical points, fixed points, and periodic points as prime governors of dynamics3. Here’s why that should surprise you: If \(f: \mathbb{C} \rightarrow \mathbb{C}\) is holomorphic and say you know the zeroes and poles of \(f\). Basic one variable complex analysis will tell you that you can by and large determine the function \(f\). To be specific, if \(z_0\) were a zero, then if you know \(\{f^{(n)}(z_0)\}_n\). You know that, \[f(z) = \sum_{n \geq 0}^{\infty}{\frac{f^{(n)}(z_0)}{n!}(z-z_0)^n}\] on a disk that extends upto the nearest pole to \(z_0\). Furthermore, if \(f\) is rational then its zeroes and poles determine it entirely. Yet the philosophy says that stating almost precisely what \(f\) is is not enough to study its dynamics!

Now, here’s why it shouldn’t surprise you: Let \(\phi : S \rightarrow S'\) be a biholomorphism.

If we change our coordinates via the map \(\phi\), the dynamics won’t be affected for the following two reasons:-

  1. \(\tilde{f}^{\circ n} = (\phi \circ f \circ \phi^{-1})^n = \phi \circ f^{\circ n} \circ \phi^{-1} = \widetilde{f^{\circ n}}\)

  2. If \(\{f^{\circ n}_{\big|U}\}_n\) is normal then so is \(\{\tilde{f}^{\circ n}_{\big|\phi(U)}\}_n\)

So, naturally, in order to study dynamics one must look for things that are invariant under coordinate transformations. Zeroes and poles are not among such invariants, as can easily be seen: If \(f(z_0) = 0\), then \(\tilde{f}(\phi(z_0)) = \phi(0)\), which need not always be \(0\), and similarly with poles. But, if \(\hat{z}\) is a fixed point or a critical point then:-

  1. \(\tilde{f}(\phi(\hat{z})) = \phi(\hat{z})\) (\(\phi(\hat{z})\) is a fixed point of \(\tilde{f}\)).

  2. \(\tilde{f}'(\phi(\hat{z})) = 0\) (by chain rule).

Zeroes and poles of \(f: \hat{\mathbb{C}} \rightarrow \hat{\mathbb{C}}\) are merely points that map to the two poles of the Riemann sphere. If you change your coordinates on \(\hat{\mathbb{C}}\) via a Möbius transformation \(\frac{az +b}{cz +d} \in\) PSL\(_2(\mathbb{C})\), then the zeroes and poles shall be thrown to points \(\frac{b}{d}\) and \(\frac{a}{c}\) (respectively). Therefore, saying one wants to study zeroes and poles of \(f\) is equivalent (in this case) to saying that one has a preferred set of coordinates. This though is extremely useful while doing analysis, is irrelevant for dynamics.

Having established critical points and fixed points4 as desired invariants; we shall move on and deal with them in a slightly more involved manner.

Definition 2.12

(Classification of Fixed Points)

  1. \(f(\hat{p}) = \hat{p}\) is attracting if \(|f'(\hat{p})| < 1\). (Here by \(f'(\hat{p})\) we mean the derivative of the coordinate function of \(f\).)

  2. \(f(\hat{p}) = \hat{p}\) is repelling if \(|f'(\hat{p})| > 1\).

  3. \(f(\hat{p}) = \hat{p}\) is indifferent if \(|f'(\hat{p})| = 1\).

There is a natural dilemma at this juncture. Dynamics of \(f\) and \(f^{\circ n}\) must be the same, for if \(\{f^{\circ m}_{\big|U}\}_m\) is normal, so is \(\{f^{\circ mn}_{\big|U}\}_m\). Should we focus our study on fixed points and critical points of \(f\) or should we pick a suitable iterate, \(f^{\circ 100}\) perhaps, and study its critical points and fixed points? The following two lemmas shall clear this imminent issue. Let \(f\) be a holomorphic self map on the Riemann surface \(S\).

Lemma 2.13

(Invariance of Julia Set I):- \[z \in J(f) \iff f(z) \in J(f).\]

Lemma 2.14

(Invariance of Julia Set II):- \[J(f^{\circ n}) = J(f).\]

Therefore, it doesn’t matter what iterate of \(f\) one chooses to work with as far as dynamics is concerned. To illustrate what it means to work with fixed points of \(f^{\circ n}\) and also for the sake of completeness let us have the following:-

Definition 2.15

(Periodic Orbits):- Let \(f: S \rightarrow S\), \(f \in Hol(S, S)\), then \(f: z_0 \rightarrow z_1 \rightarrow \ldots \rightarrow z_m = z_0\) with all \(z_i\) distinct is called a periodic orbit of period \(m\). Set, \[\lambda = (f^{\circ m})'(z_i) = \prod_{i = 1}^{m}{f'(z_i)}\]Then \(\lambda\) is called the multiplier of the orbit.

We shall now briefly explain the classification of attracting and repelling fixed points topologically. In the lemma that follows a crucial ingredient that goes in its proof is Schwarz’s lemma, necessitating the requirement of holomorphicity in our hypothesis.

Let \(\hat{p}\) be a fixed point of \(f\). The intuitive idea of attraction to \(\hat{p}\) is that the points surrounding it get pulled to it uniformly. Explicitly stated, \(\hat{p} \in S\) is said to be topologically attracting if \(\exists\) a neighbourhood \(U\) such that \(\{f^{\circ n}_{\big|U}\}_n\) converges uniformly to \(z \rightarrow \hat{p}\). One can similarly make sense of repulsion by expecting all orbits of nearby points to eventually escape a fixed neighbourhood of \(\hat{p}\)5. Such a fixed point will be called topologically repelling.

Lemma 2.16

(Equivalence of Topological and Analytical Attraction/Repulsion):- \(|f'(\hat{p})| > 1\) (or \(< 1\)) \(\iff\) \(\hat{p}\) is topologically repelling (or attracting).

Collect all points \(z \in S\) such that \(\{f^{\circ n}(z)\}_n\) converge to \(\hat{p}\), for an attracting fixed point \(\hat{p}\). This set shall be called the basin of attraction for \(\hat{p}\) (denoted by \(\mathcal{A}(\hat{p})\)), and in this basin the forward invariant component (i.e the component containing \(\hat{p}\)) is called the immediate basin of attraction (denoted by \(\mathcal{A}^o(\hat{p})\)). Clearly, such basins belong to the Fatou set and repelling fixed points to the Julia set. Of the indifferent fixed points, a certain kind is always dumped in the Julia set.

Definition 2.17

(Parabolic Fixed Point):- A fixed point \(\hat{p}\) is said to be parabolic if \(f'(\hat{p})\) is a root of unity, and for all \(n\), \(f^{\circ n}\) is not the identity map.

Lemma 2.18

(Points in the Julia Set):- Repelling points and parabolic points belong to the Julia set.

Let us specialize to the case \(f: \hat{\mathbb{C}}\rightarrow \hat{\mathbb{C}}\), \(f\) a rational map with deg\((f) \geq 2\), to see a glimpse of what studying dynamics is. In dynamics, more than studying stability one is interested in taming chaos, so, we shall focus relatively more on the Julia set of \(f\) in what’s to follow.

Proposition 2.19

(Chaos Exists):- \(J(f) \neq \phi\)

By definition, points in the Fatou set have locally uniform behaviour, that is, the "sizes" of the sets in the orbit of a neighbourhood of a point in the Fatou set shall turn out to be a stable (specifically bounded) sequence. Something strikingly contrary will be shown to be true for Julia sets. But before revealing that let us distinguish between periodic orbits and eventually periodic orbits.

Definition 2.20

(Grand Orbit Finite):- By a grand orbit of \(z\) under \(f: S \rightarrow S\), we mean the set GO\((f, z) := \{z' \in S|\) (orbit of \(z\)) \(\cap\) (orbit of \(z') \neq \phi\}\). A point \(z\) shall be called grand orbit finite (or exceptional) if GO\((f, z)\) is finite. The collection of all exceptional points shall be denoted by \(\mathcal{E}(f)\).

Lemma 2.21

:- All exceptional points are superattracting (as in have multiplier 0), and \(|\mathcal{E}(f)| \leq 2\).

Proposition 2.22

(Expansion):- Let \(z \in J(f)\). If N is a neighbourhood of \(z\), we have, \[\hat{\mathbb{C}}\backslash \mathcal{E}(f) \subseteq \bigcup_{n\geq0}{f^{\circ n}(N)}\] Further, equality is attained for sufficiently small \(N\).

Another way in which Julia sets (in this scenario) bring out a contrast in dynamics is by not admitting interiors.

Proposition 2.23

(Empty Interior):- Int\((J)\) \(\neq \phi\) \(\implies J(f) = \hat{\mathbb{C}}\).

Recall that basins of attractions belong to the Fatou set, they shrink upon iteration, whereas neighbourhoods of Julia sets expand. These two properties interact in the proof of the following proposition.

Proposition 2.24

:- Basin Boundary \(\subseteq\) Julia Set.

The above proposition has essentially spelled out the nature of the dynamics of \(f\). The components of the Fatou sets, like islands, are separated by a thin stream of components of the Julia set. Let us now talk about the topological structure of \(J(f)\), for the nature of the boundary shall also reveal what it bounds.

Proposition 2.25

(Topological Structure of Julia Set I):- Let \(z\) be a point in the Julia set of \(f\), we have, \[J(f) = \overline{\bigcup_{n \geq 0}{f^{-n}(z)}}\]

Proposition 2.26

(Topological Structure of Julia Set II):- Julia set has no isolated points.

Proposition 2.27

(Topological Structure of Julia Set III):- For a point \(z\) in a generic subset of \(J(f)\), the sequence \(z, f(z), f^{\circ 2}(z),...\) is dense in \(J(f)\).

Proposition 2.28

(Topological Structure of Julia Set IV):- \(J(f)\) is either connected or has uncountably many components.

Another striking feature of the Julia set is that it repeats shapes and patterns infinitely often. Mathematically speaking, say \((J(f), z)\) is locally conformally isomorphic to \((J(f), z')\) if \(\exists\) a neighbourhood of \(z, z'\), \(N, N'\) (respectively) such that there is a biholomorphism \(\phi: N \rightarrow N'\) with \(\phi(z) = z'\) and \(\phi(N\cap J) = N'\cap J\). Note that, by the density of preimages of points in \(J(f)\), points \(z\) such that \((J(f), z) \cong (J(f), z')\) is dense in \(J(f)\). Since for a rational map there are only finitely many critical points, \(f\) is locally univalent almost everywhere and hence one can keep backtracking. Because of this backtracking that one can do on a dense subset, Julia sets often look like what they look like.

Since the Julia set is non-empty and has no isolated points, the Fatou components are hyperbolic. One can now study periodic Fatou components by replacing \(f\) with a suitable iterate and procuring information from dynamics on hyperbolic surfaces. Classifying dynamics on hyperbolic surfaces in itself is not interesting because of the sheer lack of chaotic behaviour; we still do, for we have other ambitious purposes.

Theorem 2.29

(Classification of Dynamics on Hyperbolic Surfaces):- Let \(f\) be a self map on a hyperbolic surface \(S\). Exactly one of the four possibilities holds:-

  1. \(f\) has an attracting fixed point.

  2. For all compact sets \(K\) in \(S\), the iterates of \(K\) eventually exit \(K\).

  3. \(\exists n\) such that \(f^{\circ n}\) is identity.

  4. \(S \cong \mathbb{D}\), \(\mathbb{D}\backslash \{0\}\), or \(\mathbb{A}_r := \{z|\) \(1<|z|<r\}\) and \(f \equiv z \rightarrow e^{2\pi i \alpha}z\) with \(\alpha \notin \mathbb{Q}\).

Three remarks are in order. First, one can lift \(f\) to a map \(F\) between its universal covers and apply Schwarz’s lemma to get that all orbits of \(F\) converge uniformly on compacts to the zero function which then can be passed on to \(f\). Second, if \(f\) is a rational map, deg\((f) \geq 2\), with a Fatou component \(U\), such that for some \(z \in U\), \(f(z) = z\), and \(|f'(z)| = 1\). Then \(U \cong \mathbb{D}\), and \(f\) is equivalent to an irrational rotation on \(\mathbb{D}\). Reason being the following: the attracting case is off as \(|f'(z)| = 1\), the escape case is off because of compactness, the finite order case is off since the degree of \(f\) is \(\geq 2\), and finally as \(f\) admits a fixed point in \(U\), it can’t be equivalent to an irrational rotation on a punctured disk or an annulus. Such Fatou components are called Siegel Disks. If the Fatou component \(U\) is such that \(f\) on \(U\) is equivalent to an irrational rotation on an annulus, we call \(U\) a Herman ring. And it can easily be observed that the case of a punctured disk being a proper Fatou component shall never arise, for Julia sets don’t have isolated points. Third, if \(U\) were a hyperbolic forward invariant Fatou component, then the second case in the classification theorem is equivalent to the boundary convergence case described in the lemma below.

Lemma 2.30

(Convergence to a Boundary Fixed Point):- Suppose \(U\) is a hyperbolic domain of a compact Riemann surface and the self map \(f\) on \(U\) extends continuously to \(\partial U\), with atmost finite number of fixed points in \(\partial U\). If some orbit of \(f\) has no accumulation in \(U\) then all orbits in \(U\) converge to a boundary fixed point of \(f\). Further, the convergence is uniform on compacts.

One of the many ways to describe dynamics on a Fatou component is by reducing the function \(f\) to a simpler one (in the right set of coordinates). In particular, if \(U\subset S\) and \(\phi: U \rightarrow \phi(U) \subseteq \mathbb{C}\) is a biholomorphism, then of all such \(\phi\)’s we look for the one that would have \(\phi \circ f \circ \phi^{-1}\) in its simplest form. Siegel disks and Herman rings are instances of such things. Results that have the aforementioned flavour are called Linearization Theorems. One tries to turn \(f\) into as linear a function as possible. This is where the philosophy we talked of runs full throttle. Usually, one studies the behaviour of \(f\) in neighbourhoods \(U\) of certain fixed points, and orbits of critical points show up on the boundaries of largest possible \(U\). In addition to that, orbits of critical points also reveal certain topological structures of Julia sets, so do certain periodic points. Hence, fixed points and distribution of the orbits of critical points are crucial.

Understanding dynamics of \(f\) near fixed points (locally) pertains to finding a change in the coordinate system which would ease the description of orbits of \(f\). A general technique in this direction is first constructing a sequence \(\{\phi_k\}_k\) of biholomorphisms embedding a neighbourhood of a fixed point into \(\mathbb{C}\) such that \(\phi_k \circ f = g \circ \phi_{k+1}\), and then proving that \(\{\phi_k\}_k\) converges uniformly to some \(\phi\). We shall then have, \[\lim_{k \rightarrow \infty}(\phi_k \circ f) = \lim_{k \rightarrow \infty}(g \circ \phi_{k+1})\] This establishes the fact that \(\phi \circ f \circ \phi^{-1} = g\), where \(g\) is a polynomial, preferably linear.

We shall now study local behaviour of \(f\) around four types of fixed points - attracting, repelling, superattracting, and parabolic. Let \(\hat{f} = \phi \circ f \circ \phi^{-1}\) be a regular coordinate representation of \(f\) (centered around a fixed point). Notice that \(\hat{f}'(0) \notin \{0, 1\}\) \(\implies\) on domains near enough to the fixed point, \(f\) behaves like \(\hat{f}(0)z\) (or \(\lambda z\), where \(\lambda\) is the multiplier). If \(\lambda <1\), \(f\) pulls, and if \(\lambda > 1\), \(f\) pushes. If \(\lambda = \hat{f}'(0) = 0\), then locally \(\hat{f}(z) = a_nz^n + a_{n+1}z^{n+1} + \ldots\) \(\implies\) \(\hat{f}\) has a zero of order \(n\) at \(0\). In a suitable domain, \(f\) shall then behave like \((h(z)z)^n\), where \(h(z)\) is non-vanishing near \(0\), hence on a compact neighbourhood its modulus shall admit extreme values. Thus, one can expect \(f\) to locally behave (approximately) like a polynomial. If the fixed point is parabolic (i.e \(\lambda = 1\)), then one should expect a totally different local behaviour. For instance, consider \((z \rightarrow z + z^3): \mathbb{C} \rightarrow \mathbb{C}\). Evidently \(f\) throws off points \(1, -1\), and pulls close points \(i, -i\). That is, locally it seems as if points are attracted and repelled along different directions at the same time. In summary, these four types of points must be handled separately.

Theorem 2.31

(Koenig’s Coordinates):- Let \(U\) be a sufficiently small neighbourhood around a fixed point \(\hat{p}\) such that \(|\lambda| \notin \{0, 1\}\), then there exists a (unique upto multiplication by a non-zero constant) conformal embedding \(\phi: U \rightarrow \mathbb{C}\) such that \((z \rightarrow \lambda z) \circ \phi = \phi \circ f\).

Theorem 2.32

(Böttcher Coordinates):- Let \(U\) be a sufficiently small neighbourhood around a fixed point \(\hat{p}\) such that \(\lambda = 0\), then there exists a (unique upto multiplication by a \((n-1)\)st root of unity) conformal embedding \(\phi: U \rightarrow \mathbb{C}\) such that \((z \rightarrow z^n) \circ \phi = \phi \circ f\), if the order of zero of the coordinate representation of \(f\) at \(0\) is \(n\).

To do something similar for parabolic points we need to work a bit more.

Definition 2.33

(Attracting/Repelling Vectors):- Let us denote the coordinate representation of \(f\) by \(f\) itself, and say it locally has the form \(f(z) = z + az^{n+1} + O(z^{n+2})\), then \(v \in \mathbb{C}\) is called an attracting vector if \(nav^n = 1\) and the same is called a repelling vector if \(nav^n = -1\). (Note: Since \(f\) is locally invertible it can be shown that for \(f^{-1}\) the roles of attracting and repelling vectors get swapped. Also, \(nav^n = \pm 1\) has \(2n\) equally spaced solutions, hence there are \(n\) attracting and \(n\) repelling (equally spaced) vectors.

Proposition 2.34

(Attraction/Repulsion along certain Directions):- If the orbit of \(z_0\), \(\{z_k\}_k\) converges to \(0\), and \(z_k \neq 0\), \(\forall k\), then, \[z_k \sim \frac{v_j}{\sqrt[\frac{1}{n}]{k}}\] Similarly, for orbits converging to \(0\) under \(f^{-1}\).

Set \(v_j = e^{\frac{\pi i j}{n}}v_0\) \(\implies\) \(v_j\) is attracting if \(j\) is odd and repelling if it is even. So, attracting and repelling vectors sandwich each other. Further, it is expected from the proposition above that some domain in \(\Delta_j := \{re^{i\theta}v_j|\) \(r>0, |\theta| < \frac{\pi}{n}\}\) must firstly contain an orbit \(\{z_k\}_k\) and secondly must asymptotically approach \(0\) along the direction \(v_j\) for odd \(j\). Such domains are called petals. More precisely,

Definition 2.35

(Petals):- Let \(N\) be a neighbourhood of the parabolic point \(\hat{p}\) on which \(f\) is univalent. \(P \subset N\) will be called an attracting petal for \(f\) at \(\hat{p}\) if:-

  1. \(f(P) \subseteq P\)

  2. \(\{z_k\}_k\), orbit of \(z_0\) eventually enters \(P\) iff \(z_k \rightarrow \hat{p}\) along \(v_j\).

These domains (visually) look like petals around the base branch \(v_j\). Such petals exist, in fact the following theorem says something far more beautiful than substantiating mere existence.

Theorem 2.36

(Parabolic Flower):- \(\exists\) petals \(\{P_j\}_{0\leq j\leq 2n-1}\), where \(P_j\) is either attracting or repelling such that \(\{\hat{p}\} \cup P_0 \cup P_1 \cup \ldots \cup P_{2n-1}\) is an open neighbourhood of \(\hat{p}\). Further, \(P_j, P_j\cap P_{j\pm1}\) are simply connected regions (except for \(n =1\)).

Definition 2.37

(Parabolic Basin):- Let \(\mathcal{A}_j(\hat{p})\) for a parabolic \(\hat{p}\) be the set of all \(p_0\) such that \(p_0 \rightarrow p_1 \rightarrow p_2 \rightarrow \ldots\) under \(f\) goes to \(\hat{p}\) along \({v_j}\) (the \(j\)th attracting vector). It is evident from the existence of petals that there exists a connected component of \(\mathcal{A}_j(\hat{p})\) that is forward invariant which we shall denote by \(\mathcal{A}_j^o(\hat{p})\)

Theorem 2.38

(Fatou Coordinates):- For any petal \(P\) \(\exists\) (a unique upto translation) conformal embedding \(\alpha: P \rightarrow \mathbb{C}\) such that \((z \rightarrow z+1) \circ \alpha = \alpha \circ f\).

We have seen the role played by fixed points so far, now let us explain the phenomenon of critical points, but for that, we have to restrict ourselves to case of rational maps. Critical points govern the dynamics of rational maps in three significant ways:-

  1. Critical points bound the extent to which Koenigs, Fatou and Böttcher coordinates can be extended biholomorphically.

  2. Number of critical points bound the number of attracting/parabolic periodic points.

  3. It determines the shape of the Julia set.

Theorem 2.39

\(\exists\) maximal \(r\) such that \(\xi: \mathbb{D}_r \rightarrow \mathcal{A}^o\) is a holomorphic inverse of the Koenigs coordinate \(\phi\), and \(\xi(\partial \mathbb{D}_r)\) contains a critical point of \(f\).

Theorem 2.40

\(\exists\) a maximal petal \(P_{max}\) in all immediate parabolic basins such that the Fatou coordinate \(\alpha\) extends biholomorphically to \(P_{max}\) and \(f\) has a critical point on \(\partial P_{max}\). (Note: \(\hat{p}\), a parabolic fixed point being on the Julia set, shall spread its grand orbit on a dense subset bounding the maximal petal).

Corollary 2.41

Number of attracting and parabolic periodic points are finite.

Theorem 2.42

\(\exists\) maximal \(r\), \(0<r \leq 1\) such that the Böttcher coordinate \(\phi\) has a holomorphic inverse \(\xi\) on \(\mathbb{D}_r\). If \(r=1\), \(\mathbb{D} \cong \mathcal{A}^o\) and \(\hat{p}\) the superattracting fixed point shall be the only critical point in \(\mathcal{A}^o\), else \(\exists\) another in \(\mathcal{A}^o\) on \(\partial \xi(\mathbb{D}_r)\).

For the time being let us specialize further to the case of polynomials on \(\mathbb{C}\).

Definition 2.43

(Filled Julia Set):- A filled Julia set is \(\{z\in \mathbb{C}|\) orbit of \(z\) under \(f\) is bounded\(\}\) (denoted usually by \(K\), or \(K(f)\).

Let us briefly talk about the filled Julia set of a polynomial \(f(z) = a_0 + a_1z +\ldots a_dz^d\), for \(d \geq 2\). Assume WLOG that \(f\) is monic (else work with \(cf(z/c)\)). We know that one can write the filled Julia set of \(f\) as \((\mathcal{A}^o(\infty))^c\). Recall the fact that the neighbourhoods of points on the Julia set are expansive upon iteration, since iterations of neighbourhoods in the interior of the filled Julia set can’t escape itself, the boundary of the filled Julia set must be the Julia set of \(f\). It can further be observed that all the bounded Fatou components of \(f\) housed in \(K\) are simply connected.

Theorem 2.44

(Structure of Filled Julia Set):- \(K\), \(\partial K\) is connected \(\iff\) All critical points have bounded orbits.

As an instance of what has been put forth let us very briefly touch upon the study of dynamics of a parametrized family of self maps \(\{f_{\lambda}\}_{\lambda \in \Lambda}\) on a Riemann surface \(S\) for a particularly benign choice of \(S\) and \(f_{\lambda}\), namely, \(S = \mathbb{C}\), and \(f_{\lambda}(z) = z^2 + \lambda\). We know that the orbit of \(0\) under \(f_{\lambda}(z)\) crucially determines the topological shape of the Julia set of \(f_{\lambda}(z)\). In that, if the orbit is bounded then \(K(f_{\lambda}(z))\) and \(J(f_{\lambda}(z))\) shall both be connected, else they shall break apart into uncountably many components.

Definition 2.45

(Mandlebrot Set):- The Mandlebrot set \(\mathcal{M}\) is defined to be the set of all \(\lambda\) such that the orbit \(\{f_{\lambda}^{\circ n}(0)\}_n\) is bounded.

Of particular interest within this set is the set of all parameters that contain a \(p\)-attracting cycle. The following proposition kneads such parameters together into a connected component.

Proposition 2.46

(Hyperbolic Components):- Suppose there is an attracting cycle of period \(m\) for \(f_{\lambda}\), then \(\lambda \in\) Int\((\mathcal{M})\). Further, if \(\Omega\) is a component of Int\((\mathcal{M})\) containing \(\lambda\), then for all \(c \in \Omega\), \(f_c\) contains an attracting cycle of period \(m\).

At this juncture, let us remark that the beautiful images of Julia sets we see are constructed using density of grand orbits of certain points in it. The possibility of computer experimentation and illustration was a major factor in reviving this subject in addition to works of Fatou, Julia, Sullivan, Hubbard, and Thurston. With that context in mind, let us state this one theorem which shall be of importance to us later, and is also relevant at this stage, given the context of the philosophy we so elaborately illustrated with theorems.

Theorem 2.47

For a rational map \(f\) with degree at least \(2\), the closure of the set of repelling periodic points equals the Julia set of \(f\).

Having developed the theory so far, let us state its first classification theorem. The image of a Fatou component \(U\) under \(f\) is also a Fatou component. Indeed, if \(f(U) \subset U'\), where \(U'\) is some other Fatou component then given \(x \in f(U)\), \(y \in f(U)^c\cap U'\), \(\exists\) a path in \(U'\) joining \(x\) and \(y\). That path must hit \(\partial f(U)\) on its way, contradicting the fact that the Fatou set and the Julia set are disjoint. Having said this, we note that a Fatou component \(U\) can do one of the following four things:-

  1. \(f(U) = U\) (invariant Fatou component).

  2. \(f^{\circ n}(U) = U\) (periodic Fatou component).

  3. \(f^{\circ k}(f^{\circ n}(U) = f^{\circ n}(U)\) (pre-periodic Fatou component).

  4. Elements in \(\{f^{\circ n}(U)\}_n\) are pairwise disjoint. (wandering Fatou component).

Theorem 2.48

(Classification of Non-Wandering Fatou Components):- Let \(U\) be a non-wandering Fatou component then it is either a branched covering or a biholomorphic copy of some periodic Fatou component, which necessarily belongs to one of the following categories:-

  1. \(U\) is an immediate basin of attraction of some attracting cycle.

  2. \(U\) is an immediate parabolic basin of attraction of some parabolic cycle.

  3. Under a suitable iterate of \(f\), \(U\) is a Siegel disk.

  4. Under a suitable iterate of \(f\), \(U\) is a Herman ring.

References

Carleson, Lennart, and Theodore W Gamelin. 2013. Complex Dynamics. Springer Science & Business Media.
Forster, Otto. 2012. Lectures on Riemann Surfaces. Vol. 81. Springer Science & Business Media.
McMullen, Curtis T. 2016. “Complex Dynamics and Renormalization (AM-135), Volume 135.” In Complex Dynamics and Renormalization (AM-135), Volume 135. Princeton University Press.
Milnor, John. 2011. Dynamics in One Complex Variable.(AM-160):(AM-160)-. Vol. 160. Princeton University Press.
Varolin, Dror. 2011. Riemann Surfaces by Way of Complex Analytic Geometry. Vol. 125. American Mathematical Soc.

  1. This object naturally takes up the structure of a Lie group. Hence, studying discrete subgroups of certain Lie groups can yield lot of information on such classification theorems.↩︎

  2. One stunning aspect of complex dynamics is how one classification theorem can be "aged" so to speak, and be exploited to yield others. A showing example would be the Uniformization Theorem (which classifies simply-connected Riemann surfaces), can be aged to prove Pick’s Theorem (which classifies the nature of distances of holomorphic maps between hyperbolic surfaces). If one ages this further one can classify dynamics on hyperbolic surfaces. And later in the chapter we shall see how this can be used to classify periodic Fatou components.↩︎

  3. This doesn’t all apply for maps in general, at some stage one must restrict oneself to the case of rational maps, or worse, polynomials.↩︎

  4. For the same reasons even periodic orbits are important. We shall not deal with periodic orbits separately, for the theorems that are valid for fixed points shall also go through for periodic points.↩︎

  5. Here, uniformity is manifest in the demand that all the nearby points escape a fixed neighbourhood of \(\hat{p}\).↩︎

title: Scalpel, Forceps, and other Surgical Tools
excerptHtml: In this chapter we shall glimpse over the relevant aspects of the theory of quasiconformal maps and see ways in which it features in holomorphic dynamics. The content over-viewed here is dealt with in depth in (Ahlfors 2006), (Branner et al. 2014), (Hubbard 2016), and (Imayoshi and Taniguchi 2012).
html:
Scalpel, Forceps, and other Surgical Tools

In this chapter we shall glimpse over the relevant aspects of the theory of quasiconformal maps and see ways in which it features in holomorphic dynamics. The content over-viewed here is dealt with in depth in (Ahlfors 2006), (Branner et al. 2014), (Hubbard 2016), and (Imayoshi and Taniguchi 2012).

Dynamics of a given holomorphic self map \(f\) on a Riemann surface \(S\) is a topological invariant. For instance, fixed points, critical points, the nature of the periodic points - attracting, repelling, superattracting, parabolic, or non-linearizable, all remain the way it was upon one’s change of coordinates on \(S\) via a homeomorphism. The issue, as was expressed in Chapter \(1\) is that of rigidity. Conformal maps are too rigid, that is, they preserve way too much information. A biholomorphic change of coordinate preserves all the analytic parameters of the dynamics of \(f\), like the multipliers, conformal description of Fatou components, holomorphic degree, etc.

In the interest of having some flexibility we shall first introduce a way to measure how conformal a given map is, then we shall see what shall happen to the biholomorphic coordinate change function \(\phi: S \rightarrow S'\), if we reduce the extent to which it is conformal. \(\phi\) must certainly be a homeomorphism for we want the topological core of the dynamics to be preserved. But, we also expect some form of flexibility in the analytic parameters of the dynamics of \(f\). We aspire to make the definition of this proposed almost conformal maps (i.e. quasiconformal maps) in such a way that the flexibility in its conformality is connected with the flexibility in changing the analytic quantifiers of the dynamics of \(f\). Let us begin by putting a meter on a function’s conformality.

Let \(f: \mathbb{C} \rightarrow \mathbb{C}\), then \(f\) being conformal is equivalent to saying that the linear map \(df_{z_0}: T_{z_0}\mathbb{C} \rightarrow T_{z_0}\mathbb{C}\) as a \(\mathbb{R}\)-linear map is \(\mathbb{C}\)-linear (modulo appropriate identifications). If \(f: \mathbb{C} \rightarrow \mathbb{C}\) were just continuously differentiable, then, in \((dz, d\overline{z})\) coordinate frame on \(T_{z_0}\mathbb{C}\), we will have:- \[df_{z_0} = {\frac{\partial f}{\partial z}}\bigg|_{z_0}dz + {\frac{\partial f}{\partial \overline{z}}}\bigg|_{z_0}d\overline{z}\] Where \(\left({\frac{\partial f}{\partial \overline{z}}}\bigg|_{z_0}d\overline{z}\right)\) is the extra luggage obstructing \(f\) from being holomorphic. Denote the linear map given by the differential, by \(T\), and let \(T(x, y) = (X, Y)\). Fix a circle \(\{(x, y)|\) \(x^2 + y^2 = r,\) \(r>0\}\). If \(T\) is invertible we have:-

\[\begin{pmatrix} x&y \end{pmatrix}\cdot \begin{pmatrix} x\\y \end{pmatrix} = r^2 = \left(\begin{pmatrix} X&Y \end{pmatrix}(T^{-1})^T\right) \cdot \left(T^{-1} \begin{pmatrix} X\\Y \end{pmatrix}\right)\]

\[\begin{pmatrix} X&Y \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} X\\Y \end{pmatrix} = r^2\]

Now, \((T^{-1})^T(T^{-1})\) being real symmetric, admits two eigenvalues (say \(a\), \(b\)), hence \(T\) can be diagonalized, and the equation above would take the form:- \[aX^2 + bY^2 = r^2\]

Therefore, \(df_{z_0}\) pulls back an ellipse from a circle in its co-domain. If we were to remove the extra luggage then \(df_{z_0}\) would have pulled back a perfect circle. Sard’s Theorem tells us that one can pull back ellipses from circles in \(T_{f(z)}\mathbb{C}\) almost everywhere in \(f(\mathbb{C})\). In fact, similarly, one can pullback ellipses too. Set \(a = {\frac{\partial f}{\partial z}}\bigg|_{z_0}\), \(b = {\frac{\partial f}{\partial \overline{z}}}\bigg|_{z_0}\), \(\theta =\)arg\((\frac{b}{a})\), \(\alpha =\)arg\((a)\), and \(\mu_{z_0} = \frac{b}{a}\). With these, the differential takes the form:- \[df_{z_0} = |a|e^{i\alpha}(z+|\mu_{z_0}|e^{i\theta}\overline{z})\]

Clearly, \(e^{i\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)}\), \(e^{i\left(\frac{\theta + \pi}{2}\right)}\) are eigenvectors of \(df_{z_0}\) corresponding to eigenvalues \(|a|(1+|\mu_{z_0}|)\) and \(|a|(1-|\mu_{z_0}|)\). Here, \(\theta\) sets the angle of inclination of the ellipse, as a result, \(\mu(z) = \mu_z\) essentially captures the information of the ellipse (modulo scaling).

Definition 3.1

(Dilatation):- Let \(df_{z_0}\) be non-singular, and say it pulled back an ellipse \(\mathcal{E}\) at \(z_0\), then define, \[K_{z_0}(f) = \frac{1+|\mu_{z_0}|}{1- |\mu_{z_0}|}\] to be the dilatation of \(f\) at the point \(z_0\). (Note: \(K_{z_0}(f)\) is essentially the ratio of the major axis of \(\mathcal{E}\) to its minor axis, thereby capturing by what measure \(f\) deforms circles.)

Let \(\esssup_{z_0 \in \mathbb{C}}(K_{z_0}(f)) = K < \infty\). Then the value of \(K\) controls how far \(f\) is from being conformal. We propose to adopt this as the means to loosen conformality. This can be made formal by introducing Teichmüller distances and so on, but we better not. Notice that the imposition of \(f\) being of class \(C^1\) is not that motivated. It seems as if we let that in just so we could use Sard’s Theorem. Of course there are other ways to ensure that one can pullback almost everywhere, and one such way shall lead us to the first definition of quasiconformal maps.

Definition 3.2

(First Analytic Definition of Quasiconformal Maps):- A map \(\phi: U \rightarrow V\) is said to be \(K\)-quasiconformal if:-

  1. \(\phi\) is a homeomorphism.

  2. \(\phi\) is ACL (absolutely continuous on lines).

  3. \(|\partial_{\overline{z}}\phi| \leq k|\partial_{z}\phi|\), almost everywhere, where \(k = \frac{K-1}{K+1}\).

Let us briefly address why the above is sort of the right definition to make with the help of the following important lemma.

Lemma 3.3

(Gehring and Lehto):- If \(\phi\) is an open map and has partial derivatives almost everywhere then it is differentiable almost everywhere.

Notice that if \(\phi\) is ACL, and \(m = m_1 \times m_1\) (where \(m, m_1\) are Lebesgue measures on \(\mathbb{R}^2, \mathbb{R}\), respectively: An absolutely continuous function takes a measure \(0\) set in an interval to a measure \(0\) set. Let \(A_x = \{x\} \times B_x\), be such that \(m_1(B_x) = 0\) locally (say in \(U\)), where \(B_x\) is the projection of \(\{(x, y)\}_{y \in \mathbb{R}}\) \(\cap\) (the local region, \(U\)). Then by Fubini’s Theorem \(m(f(\bigcup_{x\in \pi_1(U)}A_x)) = 0\), where \(\pi_1\) is the canonical projection onto the first coordinate. Now, for absolutely continuous functions one firstly has that \(\phi\) is locally \(C^1\) (by Egoroff’s Theorem), and secondly (exploiting Sard’s Theorem for absolutely continuous functions) one has that the local images of critical points will have measure 0. \(\mathbb{C}\) being Lindelöff, can be covered by countably many such regions in which all the aforementioned niceties exist. In conjunction, these give us that \(K\)- quasiconformal maps pull back ellipses with dilatation atmost \(K\), almost everywhere. Further, if you loosen the fact that \(\phi\) is a homeomorphism, you can’t preserve dynamics, if you loosen the fact that \(\phi\) is ACL and replace it with something like - partial differentiability (almost everywhere), then you can’t ensure that the image set of critical points have measure \(0\). And finally, if you loosen the inequality \(|\partial_{\overline{z}}\phi| \leq k|\partial_{z}\phi|\), well, then you would have essentially lost the meter. Therefore, we claim that Definition 3.2 is well justified.

By Lebesgue Decomposition Theorem if \(A(E) = m(\phi(E))\), \(A\) is sigma finite and absolutely continuous with respect to the Lebesgue measure. Therefore, \[A(E) = \int_{E}J_{\phi}((z)dm + \int_{E}d\tilde{\mu}\] Or, said differently, \(dA = J_{\phi}dm + d\tilde{\mu}\), where \(\tilde{\mu} \perp m\). This gives us, \[\int_{E}J_{\phi}((x,y))dxdy \leq A(E)\] where \(J_{\phi} = |\phi_z|^2 + |\phi_{\overline{z}}|^2\) is the Jacobian of \(\phi\). And we have, \(|\phi_{\overline{z}}|^2 \leq |\phi_z|^2 \leq \frac{J_{\phi}}{1-k^2}\) \(\implies\) \(\phi_z\), \(\phi_{\overline{z}} \in \mathbf{L}^2_{loc}\). This yields the following equivalent definition of quasiconformal maps.

Definition 3.4

(Second Analytic Definition of K-Quasiconformal Maps):- A map \(\phi: U \rightarrow V\) is said to be \(K\)-quasiconformal if:-

  1. \(\phi\) is a homeomorphism.

  2. \(\phi\) has locally integrable distributional derivatives1.

  3. \(|\phi_{\overline{z}}| \leq k|\phi_z|\).

These analytic definitions are only useful to an extent. What’s more promising (with its own limitations) is the geometric definition.

Definition 3.5

(Geometric Definition of K-Quasiconformal Map):-A map \(\phi: U \rightarrow V\) is said to be \(K\)-quasiconformal if:-

  1. \(\phi\) is an orientation preserving homeomorphism.

  2. \(\frac{1}{K}\)mod\((Q) \leq\) mod\((\phi(Q)) \leq K\)mod\((Q)\), for all topological quadrilaterals \(Q\) compactly contained in the domain.

(Note: Here mod\((Q)\) usually changes from shape to shape, for a Euclidean quadrilateral it happens to be the ratio of its length to its breadth.)

Each of these definitions are relevant for different purposes. For instance, it’s obvious from the analytic definition that quasiconformality is a local property, but is extremely non-trivial to derive purely from the geometric definition. Likewise, it is easy to see from the geometric point of view that the inverse of a \(K\)-quasiconformal map is also \(K\)-quasiconformal, but not from the analytic point of view. Hence the following equivalence is relevant.

Theorem 3.6

(Equivalence of Definitions):- \(1\)st Analytic Definition \(\iff\) \(2\)nd Analytic Definition \(\iff\) Geometric Definition.

It is was clear with the \(C^1\) assumption on \(f\) that we had indeed put a meter on conformality, for one can prove that if one were to readjust \(K\) back to \(0\), one would end back in the category of holomorphic maps. But to ensure that the same is true even in the case of quasiconformal maps, one must find one’s way back to conformality adjusting back what one tweaked to begin with. Only then our venture will be of some meaning. The following extremely powerful lemma ensures that the right meter for conformility is dilatation.

Lemma 3.7

(Weyl’s Lemma):- A \(1\)-quasiconformal map is conformal.

Clubbed below are some of the basic properties of the newly introduced class of maps that shall be of relevance to us later in this chapter.

Proposition 3.8

(Properties of Quasiconformal Maps):- The following are true:-

  1. If \(\phi\) is \(K\)-quasiconformal, then so is \(\phi^{-1}\).

  2. If \(\phi_1\) is \(K_1\)-quasiconformal and \(\phi_2\) is \(K_2\)-quasiconformal, then their composition is \(K_1K_2\)-quasiconformal.

  3. \(\phi\) is \(K\)-quasiconformal iff it is locally so.

By an ellipse field on a Riemann surface \(S\), we mean a bounded measurable choice of ellipses (modulo scaling) on tangent spaces \(T_zS\) (for almost all \(z \in S\)). Such a field, as was observed before, shall be given by an essentially bounded measurable function \(\mu(z)\) (often referred to as the Beltrami form). Its modulus shall set the dilatation of the ellipses and argument the angle of inclinations. Pullbacks of the circle field from the tangent bundle of the codomain via quasiconformal maps are instances of ellipse fields, for \(\frac{\partial \overline{z}}{\partial z}(f)(z) = \mu (z)\) is measurable. It is therefore natural to ask - Do all ellipse fields show up as pullbacks? Before pouncing on the answer to this question let us observe that ellipse fields determine the geometry of the surface. They control the shape of individual tangent spaces by linking it via a linear isomorphism to the standard Euclidean space \(\mathbb{R}^2\). These deformed tangent spaces on the bundle shall also affect Riemannian metrics on the surface \(S\) thereby affecting geometry on \(S\) as a whole. Since altering geometry of a surface alters the dynamics, we shall explore if ellipse fields can be obtained as pullbacks of quasiconformal maps, for then, the choice of what the dynamics should be altered to will be in our hands; in how we choose the ellipse field, and the altered maps will be quasiconformal conjugates of a given conformal self map (we shall illustrate this soon, in detail).

Theorem 3.9

(Measurable Riemann Mapping Theorem):- Let \(S\) be a simply connected Riemann surface (\(\cong \mathbb{D}\), \(\mathbb{C}\), or \(\hat{\mathbb{C}}\)) with a Beltrami form \(\mu(z)\). There exists a quasiconformal map \(\phi: S \rightarrow \mathbb{D}\) (or respectively onto \(\mathbb{C}\) or \(\hat{\mathbb{C}}\)) such that the pullback of the circle field via \(\phi\) is the ellipse field given by \(\mu(z)\). The map \(\phi\) shall be called the integrating map for the form \(\mu\). (Circle fields are usually denoted by \(\mu_0\), and the statement about the pullback in the theorem shall be written concisely as \(\phi^*\mu_0 = \mu\). We shall stick to this notation for pullbacks of any ellipse field henceforth). Further, given a parametrized family of Beltrami forms on \(S\), \(\{\mu_{\lambda}(z)\}_{\lambda \in \Lambda}\), such that \(\lambda \rightarrow \mu_{\lambda}(z)\) is holomorphic, then one can arrange for a family of integrating maps, \(\{\phi_{\lambda}(z)\}_{\lambda \in \Lambda}\), such that \(\lambda \rightarrow \phi_{\lambda}(z)\) is holomorphic.

The theorem above is sometimes also referred to as the Integrability Theorem or simply as the Mapping Theorem. Now, let us see an elementary example in which quasiconformal maps are used to change the analytic quantifiers of the dynamics of a conformal self map. Let us start with the map \((z \rightarrow \lambda_0z):\mathbb{D} \rightarrow \mathbb{D}\). See it as a map from \(\mathbb{D}^* \rightarrow \mathbb{D}^*\) and lift it to its universal cover \(\mathbb{H}_l\) (the left half plane). So, one has,

Here, \(v_0 =\)log\((\lambda_0)\). Set \(L_v\) to be a linear map on \(\mathbb{H}_l\) given by the following expression:-

\[\zeta \rightarrow \left(\frac{v+\overline{v_0}}{v_0 + \overline{v_0}}\right)\zeta + \left(\frac{v-v_0}{v_0 + \overline{v_0}}\right)\overline{\zeta}\]

This gives us the following commutative diagram:-

Now drop the map \(\zeta \rightarrow \zeta + v\) to \(\mathbb{D}^*\) to get,

Since the whole punctured disk is evenly covered by the exponential map, one can construct a quasiconformal map \(\phi_v\) which would conjugate \(z \rightarrow \lambda_0z\) to \(z \rightarrow e^vz\), thereby managing to change the multiplier of the fixed point \(0\) from \(\lambda_0\) to any \(e^v \in \mathbb{D}^*\). The speciality of what we did is that we constructed the conjugate explicitly. One could have instead appealed to the mapping theorem that would integrate \(\mu_v = \phi_v^*\mu_0\), but then it would have been a task to prove that \(\phi_v \circ (z \rightarrow \lambda_0z) \circ \phi_v^{-1}\) is conformal. Often you don’t end up with holomorphic maps after quasiconformal conjugation. In those unlucky situations the standard (if applicable) is to look for invariant Beltrami forms. For instance, say \(g\) is a quasiconformal self map on a simply connected Riemann surface \(S\) (\(\cong \mathbb{D}, \mathbb{C}\), or \(\hat{\mathbb{C}}\)). If one can find a Beltrami form \(\mu\) such that \(g^*\mu = \mu\), then by the mapping theorem \(\exists\) \(\phi\), \(\phi: S \rightarrow X = \mathbb{D}, \mathbb{C}\), or \(\hat{\mathbb{C}}\) such that the following commutes:-

Notice that the circle field is invariant under \(f = \phi \circ g \circ \phi^{-1}\) \(\implies\) \(f\) is \(1\)-quasiconformal, which by Weyl’s lemma is forced to be conformal. In conclusion, looking for invariant Beltrami forms is one of the most rudimentary principles of surgery.

Quasiconformal surgery often involves gluing quasiconformal maps of different qualities and exploiting Mapping Theorem \(+\) Weyl’s Lemma to end back in the realm of holomorphic maps. So the actual surgery is primarily about appending two qc maps. (Refer Figure 1) For instance, if one wants to glue \(f_1\) (a \(K_1\)-qc map) to \(f_2\) (a \(K_2\)-qc map), it is natural to ask the following two questions:-

  1. Can \(f_i\) (defined on \(D_i)\) be extended with some regularity to \(\partial D_i\)?

  2. Can the maps \(\hat{f}_i\) (defined on \(\partial D_i\)) be extended with some regularity to a map \(F\) on \(D\)?

If these two questions are answered appropriately and the boundaries are thin enough (i.e have Lebesgue measure \(0\)) then one can combine the qualities of \(f_1\) and \(f_2\) with the gluing map \(F\) and turn it into a singular qc map on \(D_1 \cup D_2 \cup D\). So, let us deal with the questions by first sketching Carathéodory’s classical work on boundary extensions. Then we shall extend it to the case of qc maps; a thorough treatment of this can be found in (Pommerenke 2013).

Suppose you have a simply connected domain \(U \subset \mathbb{C}\), then by Riemann Mapping Theorem \(\exists\) \(\phi\), a conformal isomorphism \(\phi: U \rightarrow \mathbb{D}\). To capture Carathéodory’s strategy one must move away from hyperbolic geometry and adopt spherical geometry. Let \(\rho(z)|dz|\) be the spherical metric on \(\hat{\mathbb{C}}\). Impose the same on \(\mathbb{D}\) and \(U\). Consider \(I^2 \subset \hat{\mathbb{C}}\), and let \(A\) denote the area function, then, \[A(I^2) = \int_{I^2}{\rho(x+iy)^2dxdy}\]

The length of a segment \(y = C\) is given by,

\[L(y) = \int_{x\in I}{\rho(x+iy)dx}\]

and by Cauchy-Schwarz inequality we have,

\[\left(\int_{I}{\rho(+iy)dx}\right)^2 \leq \left(\int_{I}{1^2dx}\right)\left(\int_{I}{\rho(x+iy)^2dx}\right)\]

\[\implies \int_{I}{L(y)^2dy} = \mathcal{O}(A(I^2))\]

Think of \(I^2 \cong \mathbb{D}\) to conclude that for almost all radial lines \(r \rightarrow re^{i\theta}\) (\(r>0\)) in \(\mathbb{D}\),

\[\lim_{r \rightarrow 1}{\phi^{-1}(re^{i\theta})}\]

exists2 and belongs to \(\partial U\), for oscillating curves can’t have finite length.

Theorem 3.10

(Fatou, M. Riesz, F. Riesz):- For almost every point \(e^{i\theta} \in \mathbb{D}\), the image of the radial line \(r \rightarrow re^{i\theta}\) lands. However, for a fixed \(u_0 \in \partial U\), the set of \(\theta\) for which the image of the radial line \(r \rightarrow re^{i\theta}\) lands at \(u_0\) has Lebesgue measure \(0\).

So far, for almost all \(\theta \in (0, 2\pi]\), the function \(\phi^{-1}\) gives us a good candidate for \(\phi^{-1}(e^{i\theta})\). In fact, one also has the following interesting inverse statement.

Theorem 3.11

(Accesses and Radial Limits):- Let \(R\) be the Riemann map, \(R:\mathbb{D} \rightarrow U\) and \(\gamma: [0,1) \rightarrow U\) be a curve which lands at a point \(z_0\) in the boundary of \(U\). Then the curve \(R^{-1} \circ \gamma\) in \(\mathbb{D}\) lands at some point \(\zeta\) of \(\partial\mathbb{D}\), and \(R\) has the radial limit at \(\zeta\) equal to \(z_0\). Moreover, if \(\gamma_1, \gamma_2: [0,1) \rightarrow U\) are curves landing at a common point \(z_0 \in \partial U\), then \(\gamma_1\) and \(\gamma_2\) are in the same access to \(z_0\) if and only if \(R^{-1}(\gamma_1)\) and \(R^{-1}(\gamma_2)\) land at the same point in \(\partial \mathbb{D}\).

To ensure continuous extension to \(\partial U\) or \(\partial \mathbb{D}\) one must ensure that for any sequence \(\{z_j\}_j\), \(z_j \rightarrow e^{i\theta}\), one has \(\phi^{-1}(z_j) \rightarrow \phi^{-1}(e^{i\theta})\).

Definition 3.12

(Crosscuts):- By a crosscut for the pair \((U, \partial U)\) we mean a subset \(A \subset U\) homeomorphic to \((0, 1)\) whose closure is homeomorphic to \([0,1]\) with only two endpoints in \(\partial U\).

Note that \(U \cong \mathbb{D}\) and for all sequences \(\{x_i\}_i\), \(x_i \rightarrow x \in \partial U\), we have that the accumulation points of \(\{\phi(x_i)\}_i\) belong to \(\partial \mathbb{D}\). This leads to a homeomorphism, \[\tilde{\phi}: \overline{U}/\partial U \rightarrow \overline{\mathbb{D}}/\partial \mathbb{D} \cong S^2\]

Let the crosscut \(A\) be seen as a Jordan curve in \(S^2\), then by the Jordan curve theorem \(A\) will divide \(U\) into two regions \(U^+\) and \(U^-\) (the signs are assigned depending on the orientation of \(A\)). The domains \(U^+\) and \(U^-\) shall be referred to as crosscut domains.

Definition 3.13

(Fundamental Chains and Prime Ends):- By a fundamental chain \(\mathcal{N} = \{N_j\}_j\) in \(U\), we mean a nested sequence of crosscut neighbourhoods \(N_j \subset U\) such that their corresponding crosscut closures \(\overline{A_j}\) are disjoint and such that their diameters tend to \(0\). Two fundamental chains \(\{N_j\}_j\) and \(\{N_j'\}_j\) are said to be equivalent if every \(N_j\) contains some \(N_k'\) and vice versa. An equivalence class of fundamental chains is called a prime end for the pair \((\overline{U}, \partial U)\) (usually denoted by \(\mathcal{E}\)).

The following propositions spill out some basic properties of fundamental chains.

Proposition 3.14

(Properties of Fundamental Chains I):- For any fundamental chain \(\{N_j\}_j\), the intersection of open sets \(N_j\) is empty. However, the impression, \(\cap \overline{N_j}\) is a non-empty compact connected subset of \(\partial U\).

Proposition 3.15

(Properties of Fundamental Chains II):- Any two fundamental chains are either equivalent or eventually disjoint.

Proposition 3.16

(Properties of Fundamental Chains III):- Fundamental chains are conformal invariants.

In light of the propositions above the following is natural.

Definition 3.17

(Carathéodory Compactification):- Let \(\mathcal{E}\) be the prime end for \((\overline{U}, \partial U)\), then \(\hat{U}\), the compactification is defined to be:- \[\hat{U}:= U\bigsqcup\left(\bigsqcup_{\mathcal{N} \in \mathcal{E}}{\mathcal{N}}\right)\]

Having seen all this, clearly, \(\overline{\mathbb{D}} \cong \hat{\mathbb{D}} \cong \hat{U}\). So, to be able to extend continuously to the boundary one merely has to compare the topology of \(\hat{U}\) with that of \(\overline{U}\). This enabled Carathéodory to establish a criterion for continuous boundary extensions dependent only on the topological structure of the boundary of \(U\). In particular, it is independent of the map \(\phi\).

Theorem 3.18

(Carathéodory’s Theorem):- \(\phi: \mathbb{D} \rightarrow U\) a conformal isomorphism, extends continuously to the boundary \(\iff\) \(\partial U\) is locally connected.

Carathéodory’s theorem can be easily extended to the case of quasiconformal maps.

Theorem 3.19

(Carathéodory’s Theorem for Quasiconformal Maps):- \(f: \mathbb{D} \rightarrow G\) be a qc map, \(G\) a Jordan domain, then \(f\) can be extended continuously to the boundary.

In fact, something stronger can be said about the regularity of the boundary extension in the theorem above. For that, let us introduce two objects.

Definition 3.20

(Quasisymmetric Maps):- A map \(h: \mathbb{S}^1 \rightarrow \mathbb{C}\) is quasisymmetric if \(h\) is injective, and if there exists a strictly increasing continuous function \(\lambda: [0, \infty) \rightarrow [0, \infty)\) such that, \[\frac{1}{\lambda \left(\left|\frac{z_2 - z_3}{z_1-z_2}\right|\right)} \leq \left|\frac{h(z_1)-h(z_2)}{h(z_2)-h(z_3)}\right| \leq \lambda \left(\left|\frac{z_1-z_2}{z_2-z_3 }\right|\right)\]

\(\forall\) \(z_1, z_2, z_3 \in \mathbb{S}^1\).

Definition 3.21

(Quasiarcs):- A Jordan curve \(\gamma\) is called a quasiarc if \(\exists\) \(C>0\) such that the diameter of the smaller arc of \(\gamma\) joining \(z_1\) and \(z_2\) is dominated by \(C|z_1 - z_2|\) (\(\forall\) \(z_1, z_2 \in \gamma\)). If the curve is closed, we shall call it a quasicircle, and the domains bounded by quasicircles shall be called quasidiscs.

Proposition 3.22

(Composition of Quasisymmetric Maps):- Let \(h_1, h_2\) be quasisymmetric maps. Then:-

  1. If \(h_1(\mathbb{S}^1) = \mathbb{S}^1\) \(\implies\) \(h_2 \circ h_1\) is quasisymmetric.

  2. If \(h_1(\mathbb{S}^1) = h_2(\mathbb{S}^1)\) \(\implies\) \(h_2^{-1}\circ h_1\) is quasisymmetric.

Having introduced these objects let it be noted that the boundary extension in Theorem \(3.19\) is quasisymmetric. This takes care of the first of the two questions raised before as satisfactorily as the answer given by Carathéodory for conformal boundary extensions did. In the interest of answering the second question and also connecting the two objects that were just introduced, let us state two theorems.

Theorem 3.23

(Domain to Boundary):- Let \(G\) be a Jordan domain, \(\gamma := \partial G\), and let \(f: \mathbb{D} \rightarrow G\) be a conformal isomorphism, then \(f\) admits a quasisymmetric extension to \(\mathbb{S}^1\) \(\iff\) \(\gamma\) is a quasicircle.

Theorem 3.24

(Boundary to Domain):- Let \(f:\mathbb{S}^1 \rightarrow \mathbb{S}^1\) be an orientation preserving quasisymmetric homeomorphism. Then \(\exists \hat{f}\), \(\hat{f}: \overline{\mathbb{D}} \rightarrow \overline{\mathbb{D}}\) such that \(\hat{f}\big|_{\mathbb{D}}\) is quasiconformal.

The problem of filling up domains quasiconformally by somehow interpolating boundary maps are essentially resolved by theorems like Theorem \(3.24\) for domains other than the unit disk. But saying something for a general domain is difficult, for we don’t have the tools to capture all its analytic qualities. Most of these domain extensions use quite a lot of analytic properties of the domains, of them all, perhaps the most crucial is in making choices about certain covering spaces it admits. We however have annular versions of Theorem \(3.23\) and Theorem \(3.24\), and it shall suffice for our purposes.

Theorem 3.25

(Annular Version of Theorem \(3.23\)):- Let \(A\) be a Jordan annulus, \(\mathbb{A}_r\), the standard annulus bounded by the unit circle and the circle of radius \(r\), and \(f:\mathbb{A}_r \rightarrow A\) a conformal isomorphism. Let \(\gamma^i\) and \(\gamma^o\) denote its inner and outer boundaries. Then \(f\) has a quasisymmetric extension to \(\mathbb{S}^1\), \(S_r^1\) \(:= \{z|\) \(|z| = r\}\) \(\iff\) \(\gamma^i\) and \(\gamma^o\) are both quasicircles.

Theorem 3.26

(Annular Version of Theorem \(3.24\)):- For \(0<r_1<r_2<1\), let \(f_1:\mathbb{S}^1 \rightarrow \mathbb{S}^1\), \(f_2:\mathbb{S}^1_{r_1} \rightarrow \mathbb{S}^1_{r_2}\) be two orientation preserving quasisymmetric homeomorphisms \(\implies\) \(\exists\) \(f\), \(f: \overline{\mathbb{A}}_{r_1}\rightarrow \overline{\mathbb{A}}_{r_2}\) such that its restriction on \(\overline{\mathbb{A}}_{r_1}\) is quasiconformal.

Having laid out the theory necessary for surgical constructions let us briefly reiterate it by listing the essential tools one would need. In order, they are:-

  1. Measurable Riemann Mapping Theorem. It shall play the role of a scalpel by instigating any surgical procedure.

  2. Invariant Beltrami Forms will be our forceps, holding the incision for as many deformations as one would desire.

  3. Theorems on Boundary and Domain Extensions shall be the actual tools that one would need to fundamentally change the nature of a self map.

  4. Weyl’s Lemma shall become sutures by helping us land back in the realm of holomorphic maps; putting an end to the alterations.

Now, there are certain rules to follow. One should know when these tools can successfully be applied, and that too in the order that they have been listed above. For that, we have the following theorems which shall in some sense be our principles. The theorems illustrate instances where some of these tools can be applied, hence we shall call them surgical principles3.

Theorem 3.27

(Principle I):- If \(\Gamma\) is a quasiarc and \(\phi: U \rightarrow V\), a homeomorphism that is \(K\)-qc on \(U\backslash \Gamma\). Then \(\phi\) is \(K\)-qc on \(U\). (Note: As a consequence, if the boundary pieces are regular enough, one can construct global qc maps by gluing them along such boundary pieces).

Theorem 3.28

(Principle II):- Let \(U \subset \mathbb{C}\) be open, \(C \subset U\) compact, \(\phi\) and \(\Phi\) two mappings \(U\rightarrow \mathbb{C}\) which are homeomorphisms. Suppose \(\phi\) is qc, and so is \(\Phi\) on \(U\backslash C\), and that \(\phi = \Phi\) on \(C\). Then \(\Phi\) is quasiconformal. (Note: This is referred to as Rickman’s Lemma).

Theorem 3.29

(Principle III):- \(f: \hat{\mathbb{C}} \rightarrow \hat{\mathbb{C}}\) be quasiconformal. If \(\exists\) \(K\), such that \(f^{\circ n}\) is \(K\)-qc, \(\forall n\), \(n \geq 1\). Then \(f\) is quasiconformally conjugate to a rational map. (Note: In literature, this is called the Straightening Theorem. It informs us of when the incision done on \(f\) can lead us to a situation where Weyl’s Lemma can be applied).

Here we conclude our discourse on the preliminaries. In the chapters to follow we shall see three fundamentally different instances of quasiconformal surgery in complex dynamics.
